summary: The lecture defines geography and its branches, then explains seven major hypotheses on the origin of Earth and the solar system: Gaseous (Kant), Nebular (Laplace), Planetesimal (Chamberlain-Moulton), Tidal (Jeans-Jeffreys), Binary Star (Russell), Supernova (Hoyle), and Interstellar Dust (Schmidt). It stresses hand-drawn diagrams for exam readiness.
points: Geography term coined by Eratosthenes from Greek 'geo' (earth) and 'graphos' (description).
Branches: Physical (geomorphology, climatology, biogeography, pedology, oceanography) and Human (historical, political, economic, social, cultural, population, thought).
Gaseous Hypothesis: Kant (1755) – cold solid primordial nebula; collision generates heat, rotation; residue forms Sun, accretion forms planets.
Nebular Hypothesis: Laplace (1796) – hot rotating nebula cools, contracts, spins faster; centrifugal force ejects rings forming planets.
Planetesimal Hypothesis: Chamberlain & Moulton (1905) – proto-Sun and companion star; tidal force pulls planetesimals; accretion forms planets.
Tidal Hypothesis: Jeans & Jeffreys – stationary rotating proto-Sun; intruding star's tidal force ejects cigar-shaped filament forming planets.
Binary Star Hypothesis: Russell (1937) – three bodies: proto-Sun, companion star, approaching star; material pulled from companion forms planets.
Supernova Hypothesis: Hoyle – companion star explodes as supernova; debris accretes around proto-Sun forming planets.
Interstellar Dust Hypothesis: Otto Schmidt – Sun surrounded by dust cloud; cloud revolves, particles accrete into planetesimals then planets.
Quantitative Revolution: application of mathematical/statistical techniques in geography.
